items.title: Your cell membranes are 200,000 volts per centimetre
items.claim: The inner mitochondrial membrane has a voltage of about 150 mV across its 5-nanometre thickness. Scaled up, that's an electric field of 30 million volts per metre — strong enough to ionise air. Cells run their lives in fields this intense.
items.prompt: Why is the membrane voltage so high?

options.text: The proton motive force has two components — pH gradient (~1 unit) and electrical potential (~150 mV) — and together they store the energy released by respiration in a form that ATP synthase can harvest
Mitochondria conduct electricity for the cell
Voltage is needed for genetic material to fold

items.reveal:
Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory unified electron transport with ATP synthesis through the proton motive force (PMF). Total PMF (the cell's 'fuel gauge') = chemical potential of proton gradient + electrical potential of charge separation.

Magnitudes in mitochondria: pH gradient is about 0.7 units (intermembrane space more acidic), membrane potential about -150 to -180 mV (matrix is negative). Together: ~200 mV of PMF, or ~20 kJ/mol of proton transferred.

The field strength (~3 x 10^7 V/m) inside the membrane is comparable to lightning. Life happens at electric fields that humans only experience during catastrophes.

Across thylakoid membranes (chloroplasts), the gradient is mostly chemical (pH 5 vs 8) rather than electrical.

Disrupting PMF with uncouplers, ionophores or cyanide kills cells in seconds — the gradient must be continuously rebuilt to maintain ATP synthesis.
items.why: Cells seem soft and slow. The energy machinery within them runs at field strengths that would shatter rigid materials. Life depends on holding lightning-scale electricity inside membranes of fat.

items.title: Sea otters maintain entire underwater forests
items.claim: Where sea otters live, kelp forests thrive. Where they have been hunted to near-extinction, sea urchins explode and graze kelp to bare rock ('urchin barrens'). One otter eats about 25% of its body mass in urchins daily.
items.prompt: What makes otters a keystone species?

options.text: They are the largest predators present
They selectively eat sea urchins, the only major kelp grazer in the system; removing otters releases urchin populations, which devastate kelp forests that support hundreds of other species
Otters fertilise the water with their waste

items.reveal:
Jim Estes and John Palmisano (1974) compared Aleutian islands with otters to islands where otters had been wiped out for the fur trade. The contrast was startling: lush kelp forests vs barren urchin-grazed rock.

Kelp forests are enormously productive. They support fish, invertebrates, sea birds, marine mammals. They sequester carbon. They dampen wave energy and protect coasts.

Subsequent work (Estes et al. 1998) suggested that killer whale predation on sea otters — possibly because their normal prey, large whales, had been depleted by whaling — was driving a SECOND collapse of Aleutian otter populations, with knock-on collapses of kelp.

A whaling-era extinction cascade may still be propagating decades later. Ecosystems have memory.

The 'keystone species' concept (Paine 1969) was based on starfish; otters became its most famous illustration. Many ecosystems have keystones; identifying them before they collapse is a recurring conservation challenge.
items.why: Big effects from one species seem improbable. In sea otter ecosystems, the entire architecture depends on one mid-sized predator preventing one herbivore from grazing the forest down.

items.title: Your kidneys filter 180 litres of blood plasma every day
items.claim: Each kidney has about a million nephrons. Together they filter 125 ml of plasma per minute — 180 litres per day. Your final urine output is 1 to 2 litres. The kidneys reabsorb 99% of what they filter.
items.prompt: Why filter so much only to put it back?

options.text: Bulk filtration is the only way to expose all blood-borne solutes to selective reabsorption; the kidney keeps what's needed (glucose, salts, amino acids, water) and lets the rest go — fine selectivity requires high throughput
The body has extra water to spare

items.reveal:
The glomerulus is a knot of capillaries inside a Bowman's capsule. Blood pressure forces plasma (minus proteins and cells) through a selective barrier into the nephron tubule.

Flow rates: glomerular filtration rate (GFR) ~120-125 ml/min in healthy adults. Total renal blood flow ~1.2 L/min — about 20-25% of cardiac output. The kidneys take a major share of the circulation for their mass.

The filtrate then passes through the tubules. Proximal tubule reabsorbs glucose, amino acids, most salts, water. Loop of Henle sets up an osmotic gradient. Distal tubule fine-tunes. Collecting duct adjusts water under ADH (antidiuretic hormone).

Result: 180 L filtered, 178.5 L returned to blood, 1.5 L excreted as urine.

GFR drops with age (~1% per year after 40), kidney disease, dehydration. Maintaining it is why drinking water matters — and why drugs that affect kidney function require careful monitoring.
items.why: Filtration that throws everything out and re-claims most of it sounds wasteful. It's the simplest design that ensures any potentially harmful blood-borne molecule eventually leaves the body.
